content: Bloody or tarry stools are often indicative of an injury or disorder within the digestive tract. Physicians may use the term melena to describe black, tarry, and foul-smelling stools, or hematochezia to refer to red or maroon-colored stools. Blood in the stool can originate from any part of the digestive tract, ranging from the mouth to the anus. In some cases, the blood may be present in such small amounts that it is not visible to the naked eye and can only be detected through a fecal occult blood test. Black stools typically suggest that the bleeding is occurring in the upper gastrointestinal (GI) tract, which includes the esophagus, stomach, and the first part of the small intestine. Blood exposed to digestive enzymes as it moves through the intestines often takes on a tar-like appearance. On the other hand, maroon-colored stools or bright red blood usually indicate bleeding from the lower GI tract, such as the large bowel, rectum, or anus. However, rapid or massive bleeding in the stomach can also result in bright red stools. Causes of Bloody or Tarry Stools Upper GI Tract Causes (Black Stools): Abnormal blood vessels (vascular malformation). A tear in the esophagus caused by forceful vomiting (Mallory-Weiss tear). Bleeding from stomach or duodenal ulcers. Inflammation of the stomach lining (gastritis). Insufficient blood flow to the intestines (bowel ischemia). Trauma or ingestion of a foreign body. Enlarged, overgrown veins (varices) in the esophagus or stomach. Lower GI Tract Causes (Maroon or Bright Red Stools): Anal fissures. Bowel ischemia (when blood supply to part of the intestines is cut off). Colon polyps or colon cancer. Diverticulosis (abnormal pouches in the colon). Hemorrhoids (a common cause). Inflammatory bowel disease (e.g., Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis). Intestinal infections (e.g., bacterial enterocolitis). Small bowel tumors. Trauma or ingestion of a foreign body. Vascular malformations (abnormal collections of blood vessels, such as arteriovenous malformations or AVMs). Certain foods and substances can also mimic the appearance of bloody stools. For example, consuming black licorice, lead, iron supplements, bismuth-containing medications (e.g., Pepto-Bismol), or blueberries can cause black stools. Similarly, beets and tomatoes may make stools appear reddish. In such cases, a chemical test of the stool can confirm whether blood is present. Bleeding in the esophagus or stomach, such as from peptic ulcer disease, may also cause vomiting of blood. When to Seek Urgent Medical Care You should contact your doctor immediately if you notice blood in your stool or any changes in stool color. Even if you suspect hemorrhoids as the cause, it is essential to have a medical evaluation to rule out more serious conditions. In children, a small amount of blood in the stool is usually not serious and is often caused by constipation or milk allergies. However, it is still important to report this to a doctor, even if no further evaluation is required. Treatment Options If significant blood loss has occurred, emergency treatment may be necessary. This can include: Blood transfusions. Administration of intravenous fluids. Interventional radiography embolization (a procedure to block bleeding blood vessels). Medications to reduce stomach acid. Surgery, if bleeding does not stop. Diagnosis Your doctor will take a detailed medical history and perform a physical examination, focusing on the abdomen and rectum. Questions may include: Are you taking blood thinners (e.g., aspirin, warfarin, clopidogrel) or NSAIDs (e.g., ibuprofen, naproxen)? Have you experienced any trauma to the abdomen or rectum, or accidentally swallowed a foreign object? Have you consumed black licorice, lead, Pepto-Bismol, or blueberries? Have you had more than one episode of blood in your stool? Is every stool affected? Have you experienced recent weight loss? Is there blood only on the toilet paper? What color is the stool? When did the symptoms begin? Are there other symptoms, such as abdominal pain, vomiting blood, bloating, excessive gas, diarrhea, or fever? If there is enough blood to alter the stool's appearance, the doctor will want to know the exact color to help identify the bleeding site. Diagnostic tools may include endoscopy or specialized X-ray studies. Treatment will depend on the cause and severity of the bleeding. For severe cases, hospitalization may be required for monitoring and evaluation. In cases of massive bleeding, intensive care and possibly a blood transfusion may be necessary. Diagnostic Tests The following tests may be performed to determine the cause of bloody or tarry stools: Angiography. Barium studies. Bleeding scan (nuclear medicine). Blood tests, including a complete blood count (CBC), serum chemistries, and clotting studies. Colonoscopy. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD). Stool culture. Tests for Helicobacter pylori infection. Abdominal X-rays.
